summary: Specifies AES-CMAC, an authentication algorithm that uses the CMAC mode from NIST with 128-bit AES. The document makes it conveniently available to the Internet community. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret stamp made from a scrambler. Only people who know the secret key can make the right stamp, so it shows a message has not been changed.

subtitle: A message authentication code built from the AES block cipher with a single 128-bit key.

tldr.problem: Systems that have AES available but no hash function need a way to detect both accidental and deliberate changes to a message.
tldr.mechanism: AES-CMAC runs AES in a chained CBC-MAC over the message blocks. The last block is first XORed with one of two subkeys derived from the key, and the final AES output is the MAC.
tldr.outcome: It gives a keyed integrity and authenticity check with a goal similar to HMAC. The RFC is informational and is not an Internet standard.

today: RFC 4493 is an Informational RFC. The metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why AES-CMAC Exists
sections.content:
RFC 4493 specifies AES-CMAC, an authentication algorithm based on the CMAC mode that NIST specified, used with 128-bit AES. CMAC is equivalent to OMAC1, which improved on XCBC, which in turn improved on the basic CBC-MAC. The purpose of the memo is to make AES-CMAC conveniently available to the Internet community.

A checksum or error-detecting code only catches accidental changes. A CMAC is designed to catch intentional, unauthorized changes as well. The RFC says AES-CMAC reaches a security goal similar to HMAC, and is a good fit for systems where AES is more readily available than a hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal check number only notices honest mistakes. This stamp also notices when someone sneaky changes the message on purpose.

sections.title: How the Algorithm Works
sections.content:
AES-CMAC takes a secret key K, a message of variable length and its length in octets. It returns a fixed-size MAC called T. The core is a basic CBC-MAC: each 128-bit block is XORed with the previous AES output and then encrypted.

The last block gets special treatment. If the message length is a positive multiple of the 128-bit block size, the last block is XORed with subkey K1. Otherwise it is padded with a single 1 bit followed by zero bits (written 10^i) and XORed with K2. An empty message is allowed and is treated as one incomplete block.

The MAC is 128 bits by default. It may be truncated, keeping the most significant bits, but the length must be fixed before communication starts and must not change during the lifetime of the key. Following NIST, at least a 64-bit MAC should be used as protection against guessing attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is cut into pieces and each piece is scrambled together with the result of the one before. The last piece gets an extra secret twist so a short last piece cannot be confused with a full one.

sections.title: Subkey Generation
sections.content:
Two subkeys, K1 and K2, are derived from the key K. First AES-128 is applied to an all-zero 128-bit block to give L. Then K1 is L shifted left by one bit, with the constant const_Rb (0x87 in the last byte) XORed in when the top bit of L was 1.

K2 is derived from K1 the same way: shift left by one bit, and XOR with const_Rb when the top bit of K1 was 1. Both subkeys are 128 bits (16 octets) long and are used in both MAC generation and verification.
sections.plainLanguage: From one secret key, the algorithm makes two more secret keys by scrambling a block of zeros and nudging the bits over. One extra key is for full last pieces and one for short ones.

sections.title: Generating and Verifying a MAC
sections.content:
To generate a MAC, the sender computes the subkeys, works out the number of blocks n (rounding up the length divided by 16), prepares the last block with K1 or K2, and runs the CBC chain starting from an all-zero value. The final AES output is T.

Verification is simply recomputation. The receiver runs the same generation algorithm on the message with the shared key and compares the result with the received MAC. Equal means VALID, otherwise INVALID. An invalid result means the message is definitely not authentic. A valid result gives assurance that it is authentic, though like any MAC this assurance is not absolute.
sections.plainLanguage: To check a message, you make your own stamp with the same secret key and see if it matches. If it does not match, something is wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Test Vectors
sections.content:
The security of AES-CMAC rests on AES, but also on the secrecy of the key and on correct implementations in every participating system. If the key is compromised or shared inappropriately, there is neither authentication nor integrity. The key must be generated to meet the pseudo-randomness requirements of RFC 4086 and be kept safe.

The RFC includes test vectors identical to those in NIST SP 800-38B: the subkeys for one key, and MACs for messages of length 0, 16, 40 and 64 octets. An appendix contains C code that produces them, which the RFC says is not intended for use in commercial products.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp is only as safe as the secret key. If someone steals the key, they can make perfect fake stamps. The RFC also gives practice examples so people can check their work.
